title: Interacting Galaxy Pair Arp 87
caption: The interacting galaxy pair Arp 87, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Arp 87 · constellation Leo · about 300 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Two galaxies hang side by side, joined by a twisting bridge of material. On the right is NGC 3808, the larger of the pair, a spiral seen almost face-on with a bright star-forming ring and several prominent dusty arms. On the left is its companion, NGC 3808A, a spiral seen edge-on. Together they make up Arp 87, about 300 million light-years away in the constellation Leo.

Stars, gas and dust streaming out of NGC 3808 wrap around its neighbor like an extra arm. The corkscrew shape of this shared bridge suggests that the smaller galaxy's gravity has captured some stars and gas pulled from the bigger one, and both have been bent out of shape by their mutual pull. NGC 3808A is also circled by a rotating ring of stars and gas clouds set at right angles to its disc, a feature called a polar ring.
Halton Arp cataloged the pair in the mid-1960s, from photographs that could not show the fine structure Hubble now resolves.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 combined blue, green, red and infrared filters, with F450W shown in blue, F555W in green, and hydrogen-alpha (F656N) plus near-infrared (F814W) in red.
understand.eye: Part of the red channel is near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and 6.3 hours of exposure gather far more light than an eye ever could.

behind.people: See full credit: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)
behind.exposure: Observation dates per NASA: February 2007, Exposure Time: 6.3 hours.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Interacting galaxies often form stars at high rates, a conclusion backed by the colors of their starlight, by emission from interstellar gas and by far-infrared glow from warmed dust. One of Hubble's early findings was that such galaxies hold many super star clusters, which are more compact and richer in young stars than clusters near the Milky Way.
sources: NASA release: ‘Dancing with the Stars’ Takes on a Whole New Twist
alt: Two galaxies side by side, a larger spiral with a bright ring on the right and an edge-on galaxy on the left, linked by a curving arm of material.
